prompt: Some people argue that offenders who have committed non-violent crimes should serve their sentences in the community rather than in prison. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Prison populations have grown steadily in many countries while reoffending rates have not fallen, which has revived the argument for dealing with non-violent offenders outside custody. I broadly agree with this, though the case rests on effectiveness rather than on leniency, and it does not extend to every non-violent crime.

The first reason concerns reoffending. A short custodial sentence is long enough to cost someone a job, a tenancy and often a set of family relationships, but far too short for any meaningful rehabilitation. The person released is therefore less employable and more isolated than the person imprisoned, which is close to an ideal set of conditions for further offending. A community order preserves precisely the ties that make going straight possible.

The second reason is cost. Imprisonment is among the most expensive things a state does per head, and the money buys containment rather than the supervision, treatment and unpaid work that community sentences deliver far more cheaply.

There is a serious objection, however, which is that the public often reads a community sentence as no sentence at all, and confidence in the courts is not a trivial consideration. Some non-violent crimes — large-scale fraud, corruption by officials — cause damage on a scale that seems to demand custody whatever the physical harm involved. Sentencing has an expressive function as well as a practical one, and a system that ignored this would forfeit the public consent it depends on.

My position, then, is that community sentences should be the default for low-level non-violent offending, with imprisonment reserved for cases where the harm or the breach of trust is severe. The test ought to be the seriousness of the offence, not simply whether force was used.
title: Community sentences instead of prison
